question: What is the main difference between primary and secondary heart tumours?

options.A: Secondary tumours never affect heart valves
options.B: Primary tumours are always malignant growths
options.C: Primary tumours start directly inside the heart tissues
options.D: Secondary tumours only occur in children

explanation: Primary cardiac tumours originate within the heart itself, whereas secondary tumours spread to the heart from other parts of the body. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h1)

question: How do heart tumours usually cause problems with normal heart function?

options.A: By blocking blood flow and damaging valves
options.B: By instantly causing complete electrical heart block
options.C: By destroying red blood cells in the ventricles

explanation: Tumours inside the heart chambers or walls physically block blood movement and interfere with valve closure. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h1)

question: What is the most common type of primary heart tumour in adults?
explanation: Myxomas represent the majority of primary heart tumours, most often found in the left atrium. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h2)

question: A patient has an angiosarcoma of the heart. Which chamber is most commonly involved?
explanation: Malignant primary cardiac angiosarcomas show a strong preference for the right-sided heart chambers, particularly the right atrium. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h2)

question: Which type of cancer most commonly spreads (metastasizes) to the heart?
explanation: Lung malignancies are the leading cause of secondary, metastatic cardiac involvement in clinical practice. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h3)

question: Secondary heart tumours most frequently involve which layer of the heart?
explanation: Secondary cancer cells typically travel to the pericardial space, frequently resulting in fluid accumulation around the heart. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why can symptoms of a heart tumour look like other conditions such as mitral stenosis?

options.A: Because all cardiac growths alter the electrical conduction system
options.B: Because tumours always cause high blood pressure
options.C: Because tumours can physically block blood flow through heart valves
options.D: Because secondary tumours immediately destroy heart muscle cells

explanation: An atrial myxoma can sit over the mitral valve, mimicking valvular stenosis by blocking blood flow into the ventricle. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h4)

question: Which symptom category includes unexplained fever, tiredness, and weight loss in a patient with a heart tumour?
explanation: Tumours can release inflammatory proteins into the bloodstream, producing systemic signs that resemble chronic infection or malignancy. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is the first and most common imaging tool used to check for heart masses?
explanation: An echocardiogram is non-invasive, widely available, and highly effective for visualizing heart chambers and masses. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why might a doctor order a cardiac MRI along with an ultrasound when investigating a heart tumour?

options.A: To check for blockages inside the coronary arteries only
options.B: To better show tissue details and the exact borders of the mass
options.C: To measure the electrical activity of the heart muscle
options.D: To instantly dissolve blood clots around the tumour

explanation: Cardiac MRI provides detailed tissue characterization to help differentiate between benign and malignant lesions. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is the standard treatment to completely remove a primary benign heart myxoma?
explanation: Surgically removing a benign primary tumour prevents dangerous complications like stroke or sudden cardiac death. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h6)

question: How are secondary, spreading heart tumours usually managed in patients?

options.A: With routine antibiotics to prevent infection
options.B: With electrical shock to restore normal heart rhythm
options.C: With supportive therapy and treatment targeting the primary cancer
options.D: With immediate heart transplantation as the first choice

explanation: Because secondary tumours represent widespread disease, management focuses on comfort, symptom relief, and treating the primary cancer source. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why is continuous heart monitoring (telemetry) essential after a patient has surgery to remove a heart tumour?

options.A: To watch for irregular heartbeats caused by touching the heart muscle during surgery
options.B: To prevent the myxoma tissue from growing back in the atrium
options.C: To evaluate how well the lungs are taking in oxygen
options.D: To measure the exact pumping power of the left ventricle

explanation: Surgical work on heart tissue frequently irritates the conduction system, increasing the risk of post-operative heart rhythm disturbances. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h7)

question: What critical assessment should a nurse perform regularly to check for blood clots breaking loose after heart surgery?

options.A: Inspecting the surgical wound for skin redness
options.B: Listening to bowel sounds in all four quadrants
options.C: Checking peripheral pulses and neurological status
options.D: Measuring the patient's waistline every four hours

explanation: Monitoring neurological signs and limb perfusion helps identify any debris or micro-emboli dislodged during the operation. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h7)

question: What is the typical long-term outlook for a patient who has a benign heart myxoma successfully removed?

options.B: Uncertain, because they always spread later
options.C: Poor, leading quickly to organ failure
options.D: Excellent, with high long-term survival rates

explanation: Complete surgical removal of a benign myxoma typically cures the condition and restores normal life expectancy. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h8)

question: Which of the following is NOT a typical complication of malignant heart tumours?

options.A: Bits of the tumour breaking off and blocking blood vessels
options.B: Complete natural disappearance of the tumour without treatment
options.C: Severe heart failure due to heart muscle damage
options.D: Dangerous irregular heartbeats leading to cardiac arrest

explanation: Malignant cardiac tumours do not spontaneously disappear; instead, they progress and cause heart failure, arrhythmias, and emboli. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T8#GNS213_U1_T8_h8)
